## tls.cert.expiring

**Certificate expires soon** · passive · default severity **medium**

The host's certificate expires within 21 days (within 7 days: high severity). Once it expires, browsers and clients refuse to connect.

**How to fix:** Renew the certificate, and automate renewal (ACME) so it doesn't depend on someone remembering.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8555>

## tls.cert.hostname_mismatch

**Certificate doesn't cover the host name** · passive · default severity **high**

The certificate the host presents is not valid for its name, typically because the www or apex name is missing from the certificate, or the name is served by a default virtual host.

**How to fix:** Issue a certificate whose subject alternative names include this host name, and make sure the server selects it for this name (SNI).

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6125>

## tls.cert.invalid

**Certificate is not trusted** · passive · default severity **high**

The host's certificate chain doesn't verify against the public roots: it is expired, self-signed, issued by an untrusted CA, or the server doesn't send the intermediate certificates. Browsers show a full-page warning, and API clients refuse to connect.

**How to fix:** Install a certificate from a public CA (e.g. Let's Encrypt) and configure the server to send the full chain (leaf plus intermediates). Renew expired certificates and automate renewal.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280#section-6>

## tls.cipher.weak

**Host accepts weak cipher suites** · active · default severity **medium**

The host completes handshakes that offer only cipher suites considered insecure: RC4 or 3DES (medium severity), or suites without forward secrecy (RSA key exchange) or with CBC-SHA256 (low severity). A client that prefers them gets a weak connection, and recorded RSA-key-exchange traffic can be decrypted later if the server key leaks. Seta can only offer the weak suites Go implements, so NULL and EXPORT suites aren't tested.

**How to fix:** Restrict the server to AEAD suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) with ECDHE key exchange; the Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator's "intermediate" profile is a good baseline.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7525>
- <https://ssl-config.mozilla.org/>

## tls.protocol.deprecated

**Host accepts TLS 1.0 or 1.1** · active · default severity **medium**

The host still completes handshakes with TLS 1.0 or 1.1, which RFC 8996 deprecated. They rely on weak constructions (SHA-1, CBC without AEAD) and fail PCI DSS and most audits. Seta can't test SSL 3.0 or older; use testssl.sh for that.

**How to fix:** Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1 and keep TLS 1.2 and 1.3, e.g. "ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;" in nginx.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996>

## tls.protocol.no_modern

**Host doesn't support TLS 1.2 or later** · passive · default severity **high**

Offered every version up to TLS 1.3, the host settled for TLS 1.0 or 1.1. Current browsers and most HTTP libraries no longer speak these versions and can't connect at all.

**How to fix:** Enable TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 on the server (or upgrade its TLS library).

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996>
